claim: The proportion of research outputs published in open access journals or made available on other freely-accessible platforms has increased over the past two decades.
source: The proportion of research outputs published in open access journals or made available on other freely-accessible platforms has increased over the past two decades, driven largely by funder mandates, institutional policies, grass-roots advocacy, and changing attitudes in the research community.
evidence: This is a general statement about trends in open access publishing that draws on established knowledge in the field.

claim: The increase in open access has been driven largely by funder mandates, institutional policies, grass-roots advocacy, and changing attitudes in the research community.
source: The proportion of research outputs published in open access journals or made available on other freely-accessible platforms has increased over the past two decades, driven largely by funder mandates, institutional policies, grass-roots advocacy, and changing attitudes in the research community.
evidence: This claim identifies the drivers of open access growth based on established understanding of the field.

claim: The study analyzed 1,207 institutions from across the world.
source: We studied 1,207 institutions from across the world, and found that, in 2017, the top-performing universities published around 80–90% of their research open access.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study's sample size.

claim: In 2017, the top-performing universities published around 80–90% of their research open access.
source: We studied 1,207 institutions from across the world, and found that, in 2017, the top-performing universities published around 80–90% of their research open access.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data analysis presented in the study and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Publisher-mediated (gold) open access was popular in Latin American and African universities.
source: The analysis also showed that publisher-mediated (gold) open access was popular in Latin American and African universities, whereas the growth of open access in Europe and North America has mostly been driven by repositories.
evidence: This is supported by the data analysis shown in Figure 2 and related figures.

claim: The growth of open access in Europe and North America has mostly been driven by repositories.
source: The analysis also showed that publisher-mediated (gold) open access was popular in Latin American and African universities, whereas the growth of open access in Europe and North America has mostly been driven by repositories.
evidence: This is supported by the data analysis shown in Figure 2 and related figures.

claim: There has been a large increase in the volume of publications available open access over the past decade.
source: Over the past decade, there has been a large increase in the volume of publications available open access (Piwowar et al., 2018), and this looks set to continue: indeed, a recent projection estimates that by 2025, 44% of all journal articles will be available as open access (OA) and that 70% of article views will be to OA articles (Piwowar et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Piwowar et al., 2018.

claim: By 2025, 44% of all journal articles will be available as open access.
source: Over the past decade, there has been a large increase in the volume of publications available open access (Piwowar et al., 2018), and this looks set to continue: indeed, a recent projection estimates that by 2025, 44% of all journal articles will be available as open access (OA) and that 70% of article views will be to OA articles (Piwowar et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a projection cited from Piwowar et al., 2019.

claim: By 2025, 70% of article views will be to open access articles.
source: Over the past decade, there has been a large increase in the volume of publications available open access (Piwowar et al., 2018), and this looks set to continue: indeed, a recent projection estimates that by 2025, 44% of all journal articles will be available as open access (OA) and that 70% of article views will be to OA articles (Piwowar et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a projection cited from Piwowar et al., 2019.

claim: Medical research funders in the UK, such as the Wellcome Trust and Medical Research Council, have led policy interventions for open access.
source: Medical research funders in the UK, such as the Wellcome Trust and Medical Research Council, and the National Institutes of Health in the US have led a wide range of funder policy interventions.
evidence: This is a statement about known policy interventions by these organizations.

claim: The National Institutes of Health in the US has led a wide range of funder policy interventions for open access.
source: Medical research funders in the UK, such as the Wellcome Trust and Medical Research Council, and the National Institutes of Health in the US have led a wide range of funder policy interventions.
evidence: This is a statement about known policy interventions by this organization.

claim: Universities such as Harvard University, University of Liège, and University of Southampton developed local policies and infrastructures for open access that became more widely adopted.
source: Universities such as Harvard University, University of Liège, University of Southampton and others developed local polices and infrastructures that became more widely adopted.
evidence: This is a statement about known institutional policies and their influence.

claim: In 2018, a coalition of funders set out an initiative called Plan S that requires all scholarly publications funded by public grants to be made immediately open access.
source: In 2018, a coalition of funders set out an initiative called Plan S that requires all scholarly publications funded by public grants to be made immediately open access.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the Plan S initiative.

claim: Plan S is the most ambitious, and therefore the most controversial, policy initiative to date.
source: This is the most ambitious, and therefore the most controversial, policy initiative to date with questions raised about the approach (Rabesandratana, 2019; Haug, 2019; Barbour and Nicholls, 2019), implementation details (McNutt, 2019; Gómez-Fernández, 2019; Brainard, 2019; Agustini and Berk, 2019), and unintended side effects for existing programs outside North America and North-western Europe (Debat and Babini, 2019; Aguado-López and Becerril-García, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations discussing controversies around Plan S.

claim: Questions have been raised about the approach of Plan S.
source: This is the most ambitious, and therefore the most controversial, policy initiative to date with questions raised about the approach (Rabesandratana, 2019; Haug, 2019; Barbour and Nicholls, 2019), implementation details (McNutt, 2019; Gómez-Fernández, 2019; Brainard, 2019; Agustini and Berk, 2019), and unintended side effects for existing programs outside North America and North-western Europe (Debat and Babini, 2019; Aguado-López and Becerril-García, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rabesandratana, 2019; Haug, 2019; Barbour and Nicholls, 2019.

claim: Questions have been raised about the implementation details of Plan S.
source: This is the most ambitious, and therefore the most controversial, policy initiative to date with questions raised about the approach (Rabesandratana, 2019; Haug, 2019; Barbour and Nicholls, 2019), implementation details (McNutt, 2019; Gómez-Fernández, 2019; Brainard, 2019; Agustini and Berk, 2019), and unintended side effects for existing programs outside North America and North-western Europe (Debat and Babini, 2019; Aguado-López and Becerril-García, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to McNutt, 2019; Gómez-Fernández, 2019; Brainard, 2019; Agustini and Berk, 2019.

claim: Questions have been raised about unintended side effects of Plan S for existing programs outside North America and North-western Europe.
source: This is the most ambitious, and therefore the most controversial, policy initiative to date with questions raised about the approach (Rabesandratana, 2019; Haug, 2019; Barbour and Nicholls, 2019), implementation details (McNutt, 2019; Gómez-Fernández, 2019; Brainard, 2019; Agustini and Berk, 2019), and unintended side effects for existing programs outside North America and North-western Europe (Debat and Babini, 2019; Aguado-López and Becerril-García, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Debat and Babini, 2019; Aguado-López and Becerril-García, 2019.

claim: Research outputs supported by funders that implemented monitoring and compliance checks for their policies were more likely to be published open access.
source: A recent report showed a link between the monitoring of policy and its effectiveness, demonstrating that research outputs supported by funders that implemented monitoring and compliance checks for their policies were more likely to be published open access (Larivière and Sugimoto, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Larivière and Sugimoto, 2018.

claim: Open access for works funded by Canadian funders lagged substantially even when disciplinary effects were taken into account.
source: By comparison, open access for works funded by Canadian funders, which did not monitor compliance, were shown to lag substantially even when disciplinary effects were taken into account.
evidence: This is an inference from the previous citation about monitoring and compliance.

claim: Canadian funders did not monitor compliance with open access policies.
source: By comparison, open access for works funded by Canadian funders, which did not monitor compliance, were shown to lag substantially even when disciplinary effects were taken into account.
evidence: This is stated as a fact in the context of the comparison.

claim: The SciELO project has successfully implemented an electronic publishing model for journals resulting in a surge of publisher-mediated open access.
source: For example, the SciELO project has successfully implemented an electronic publishing model for journals resulting in a surge of publisher-mediated open access (Packer, 2009; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Packer, 2009; Wang et al., 2018.

claim: For biomedical research, there was a greater level of open access for articles published from countries with a lower GDP, particularly for those in sub-Saharan Africa.
source: Recent work showed that, for biomedical research, there was a greater level of open access for articles published from countries with a lower GDP, particularly for those in sub-Saharan Africa (Iyandemye and Thomas, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Iyandemye and Thomas, 2019.

claim: For the field of Global Health, lower-ranked institutions are more likely to publish in closed outlets.
source: Meanwhile, another study showed that, for the field of Global Health, lower-ranked institutions are more likely to publish in closed outlets (Siler et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Siler et al., 2018.

claim: The tendency of lower-ranked institutions to publish in closed outlets is due to the cost of article processing charges.
source: They suggest this is due to the cost of article processing charges showing the importance of considering institutional context when examining open access performance.
evidence: This is an interpretation suggested by Siler et al., 2018.

claim: There is limited comparative and quantitative research about which policy interventions have been the most successful in promoting open access.
source: Despite the scale and success (at least in some areas) of policy interventions, there is limited comparative and quantitative research about which policy interventions have been the most successful.
evidence: This is an assessment of the state of the literature.

claim: The lack of comparative research on policy interventions is partly due to a historical lack of high-quality data on open access.
source: In part this is due to a historical lack of high-quality data on open access, the heterogeneous nature of the global scholarly publishing endeavour, and the consequent lack of any baseline against which to make comparisons.
evidence: This is an inference about the reasons for the research gap.

claim: The key to understanding and guiding the cultural changes that underpin a transition to openness is analysis at the level of research institutions.
source: We have argued (Montgomery et al., 2018) that the key to understanding and guiding the cultural changes that underpin a transition to openness is analysis at the level of research institutions.
evidence: This is an argument made by the authors in a previous publication.

claim: Choices around communication and their links to career progression and job security are strongest within researchers' professional spaces.
source: While funders, national governments, and research communities create the environments in which researchers operate, it is within their professional spaces that choices around communication, and their links to career progression and job security are strongest.
evidence: This is an inference about the importance of institutional context.

claim: Providing accurate and reliable data on open access at the university level is a challenge.
source: However, providing accurate and reliable data on open access at the university level is a challenge.
evidence: This is a statement about the difficulty of the research task.

claim: The most comprehensive work on open access at the university level currently available is that included in the CWTS Leiden Ranking.
source: The most comprehensive work on open access at the university level currently available is that included in the CWTS Leiden Ranking (Robinson-Garcia et al., 2019; Robinson-Garcia et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field supported by citations.

claim: The CWTS Leiden Ranking utilises an internal Web of Science database and data from Unpaywall to provide estimates of open access over a range of timeframes.
source: This utilises an internal Web of Science database and data from Unpaywall to provide estimates of open access over a range of timeframes.

source: These data have highlighted the broad effects of funder policies (notably the performance of UK universities in response to national policies) while also providing standout examples from regions that are less expected (for instance Bilkent University in Turkey).

claim: The CWTS Leiden Ranking has provided standout examples from regions that are less expected, such as Bilkent University in Turkey.
source: These data have highlighted the broad effects of funder policies (notably the performance of UK universities in response to national policies) while also providing standout examples from regions that are less expected (for instance Bilkent University in Turkey).
evidence: This is a statement about findings from the CWTS Leiden Ranking.

claim: The coverages of Web of Science and Scopus are biased toward the sciences and the English language.
source: For example, the coverages of Web of Science and Scopus were shown to be biased toward the sciences and the English language (Mongeon and Paul-Hus, 2016).

claim: The study gathered corresponding Crossref DOIs from the metadata of each output.
source: From this full set we gather the corresponding Crossref DOIs from the metadata of each output focusing on this set.

claim: Unpaywall was consulted to determine open access status.
source: Unpaywall is consulted to determine open access status.

claim: The study chose to combine all three datasets: Microsoft Academic, Web of Science and Scopus.

source: Secondly, we have not identified institutions individually except for those that fall within the top 100 globally for total open access, publisher-mediated open access, or repository-mediated open access.

claim: The high performance of a number of Latin American and African universities, together with a number of Indonesian universities, particularly with respect to gold open access, is striking.
source: The high performance of a number of Latin American and African universities, together with a number of Indonesian universities, particularly with respect to gold open access, is striking.

claim: The highest performers in terms of open access via repositories are dominated by UK universities.
source: The highest performers in terms of open access via repositories are dominated by UK universities.

source: This is not surprising given the power of the open access mandate associated with the Research Excellence Framework to drive university behaviour.

claim: Universities in Oceania (Australia and New Zealand) and North America (Canada and the US) lag behind comparators in Europe on repository-mediated open access.

claim: Universities in Oceania (Australia and New Zealand) and North America (Canada and the US) lag behind comparators in Latin America on publisher-mediated open access.

source: Latin American institutions show high levels of publisher-mediated open access throughout the period illustrated.

claim: The amount of additional funding from UK Research Councils relates to existing research council funding.
source: The amount of additional funding relates to existing research council funding.

source: Similarly, there was an increase in the proportion of hybrid open access publications, which largely require article processing charges, and an increase in proportion of hybrid open access within all publisher-mediated open access around the same period (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).

claim: In 2015, to be included in the UK Research Excellence Framework, universities had to deposit their research outputs in a repository.
source: In 2015, to be included in the UK Research Excellence Framework, universities had to deposit their research outputs in a repository.

claim: The UK Research Excellence Framework policy shift was profound because it relates to an assessment exercise and funding which covers all disciplinary areas, and all universities.
source: This policy shift was profound because it relates to an assessment exercise and funding which covers all disciplinary areas, and all universities.

claim: The dominance of UK universities in the top 100 for both overall open access and repository-mediated open access is potentially driven in large part by the Research Excellence Framework intervention.
source: The dominance of UK universities in the top 100 for both overall open access and repository-mediated open access, as well as the commitment to achieve 100% open access coverage being made by such a large number of universities, is potentially driven in large part by that intervention.

claim: Deals with Springer in 2015 and Wiley in 2016 in the Netherlands essentially allow authors from Dutch universities to publish their work open access in a list of hybrid journals at no cost.
source: Next, we investigated how the take up of hybrid open access publishing options in the Netherlands were influenced by deals with Springer in 2015, and Wiley in 2016 (Figure 4C). These deals essentially allow authors from Dutch universities to publish their work open access in a list of hybrid journals at no cost.
evidence: This is a statement about the nature of these publishing deals.

evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: UK research and funding council policies have been aggressive in reducing embargo lengths, mandating six months for STEM subjects and twelve months for humanities and social science subjects.
source: UK research and funding council polices have been aggressive in reducing embargo lengths, mandating six months for STEM subjects and twelve months for humanities and social science (HSS) subjects.

claim: There is evidence of different paths towards open access, depending on the context and resources.

source: However, our data suggests a fall in overall open access amongst Latin American universities from 2012 onwards, which we ascribe to an increased pressure to publish in 'international' journals that are often subscription based, and for which Latin American scholars are reluctant or unable to pay hybrid article processing charges.

claim: The fall in overall open access amongst Latin American universities from 2012 onwards is ascribed to an increased pressure to publish in 'international' journals that are often subscription based.
